content: 1. A study published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2016 (volume 10, article e0005037) presented an approach to analyzing diseases using a literature review and meta-regression, supported by a web-based software application. 2. Darzi AJ, Officer A, Abualghaib O, and Akl EA conducted a survey study in 2016, published in Health and Quality of Life Outcomes (volume 14, article 2), to assess stakeholders' perceptions of rehabilitation services for individuals living with disabilities. 3. Pion SDS, Chesnais CB, Weil GJ, Fischer PU, Missamou F, and Boussinesq M conducted a community-based study in the Republic of the Congo, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2017 (volume 17, pages 763–769), which evaluated the impact of three years of biannual mass drug administration with albendazole on lymphatic filariasis and soil-transmitted helminth infections. 4. Stolk WA, ten Bosch QA, de Vlas SJ, Fischer PU, Weil GJ, Goldman AS, and colleagues modeled the impact and costs of semiannual mass drug administration to accelerate the elimination of lymphatic filariasis. Their findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013 (volume 7, article e1984). 5. Supali T, Djuardi Y, Kaisar M, Stefanie D, Weil GJ, and Fischer P studied the effects of onceand twice-yearly mass drug administration on bancroftian filariasis and soil-transmitted helminth infections in Central Java, Indonesia. This study is registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT01905423. 6. Lindquist M provided an overview of VigiBase, the WHO Global Individual Case Safety Reports (ICSR) Database System, in an article published in Drug Information Journal in 2008 (volume 42, pages 409–419). 7. Bjerum CM, Aboulaye M, Ouattara AF, Kouadio O, Marius VK, Andersen B, and colleagues conducted a randomized clinical trial in Côte d’Ivoire comparing the effects of a single dose of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole with the standard treatment of ivermectin and albendazole for lymphatic filariasis. This study was submitted for publication in 2017 and is under review. 8. Weil GJ and King CL conducted community safety studies on the triple-drug therapy (ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole) for lymphatic filariasis as part of the Death to Onchocerciasis and Lymphatic Filariasis (DOLF) initiative. This study is registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT02899936. 9. Bolay FK, Fischer PU, and Weil GJ investigated mass drug administration for lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis in Liberia under the DOLF-Liberia program. This study is registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT01905436. 10. Meite A, Weil GJ, and Fischer PU worked on optimizing mass drug administration regimens for lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis in Côte d’Ivoire under the DOLF-Ivory Coast program. This study is registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT02032043. 11. Tafataha TT, Ngwira BM, Taegtmeyer M, Phiri AJ, Wilson TP, Banda LG, and colleagues conducted a randomized controlled clinical trial in northern Malawi to evaluate the effects of increased doses and frequency of albendazole and ivermectin on Wuchereria bancrofti microfilarial clearance. Their findings were published in Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2015 (volume 109, pages 393–399). 12. Turner HC, Osei-Atweneboana MY, Walker M, Tettevi EJ, Churcher TS, Asiedu O, and colleagues analyzed the cost of annual versus biannual community-directed treatment of onchocerciasis with ivermectin, using Ghana as a case study. Their research was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013 (volume 7, article e2452). 13. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a provisional strategy in 2012 for interrupting lymphatic filariasis transmission in loiasis-endemic countries. This report followed a meeting on lymphatic filariasis, malaria, and integrated vector management held in Accra, Ghana, from March 5–9, 2012. 14. The WHO Strategic and Technical Advisory Group for Neglected Tropical Diseases released a report in 2015 on integrating national programs to eliminate lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis. This report followed a meeting held in Geneva on February 7–8, 2015. 15. Ismail MM, Jayakody RL, Weil GJ, Nirmalan N, Jayasinghe KS, Abeyewickrema W, and colleagues evaluated the efficacy of single-dose combinations of albendazole, ivermectin, and diethylcarbamazine for treating bancroftian filariasis. Their findings were published in Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 1998 (volume 92, pages 94–97). 16. The WHO published a progress report in 2010 summarizing achievements from 2000–2009 and outlining a strategic plan for 2010–2020 for the Global Program to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis, marking the halfway point toward elimination. 17. The United Nations outlined 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) aimed at transforming the world. These goals are accessible on the UN website and were last accessed on October 20, 2017. 18. The WHO released its fourth report on neglected tropical diseases in 2017, emphasizing the integration of these diseases into global health and development initiatives. 19. Fitzpatrick C and Engels D discussed the importance of ensuring no one is left behind in achieving the SDGs, proposing neglected tropical disease indicators and tracers. Their work was published in International Health in 2016 (volume 8, supplement 1, pages i15–i18).
